lead: A grammar is ambiguous when one terminal string has two different parse trees. The string then has two meanings, and a parser cannot choose between them. This matters because programming-language grammars must give every program exactly one tree, so the compiler builds the code you intended. This chapter defines ambiguous grammar, ambiguous string and unambiguous grammar, shows the classic expression grammar with two trees for id + id × id, fixes it by layering precedence and associativity, and explains inherent ambiguity: a language is inherently ambiguous when every grammar for it is ambiguous.
prereq: You need: 3.2 Derivations and parse trees for parse trees and leftmost derivations.

blocks.text: A context-free grammar G is ambiguous if at least one terminal string w in L(G) has two different parse trees. The string w is then an ambiguous string of G. G is unambiguous if every string in L(G) has exactly one parse tree. Two parse trees always give two different leftmost derivations, so the two ideas match.
G: E → E + E | E × E | ( E ) | id
blocks.where: E is the only variable; id is an identifier terminal; +, ×, ( and ) are terminals.

blocks.text: Take the string id + id × id. Tree A uses the root rule E → E + E; its left child is id and its right child is id × id. Tree B uses the root rule E → E × E; its left child is id + id and its right child is id. Both trees have the same leaves in the same order, so both derive the one string. Thus G is ambiguous, and id + id × id is an ambiguous string of G.
E → E + T | T    T → T × F | F    F → ( E ) | id
blocks.where: E is expression, T is term, F is factor; id is an identifier.

blocks.text: A string at E level is a sum of one or more terms. A term is a product of one or more factors. A factor is an id or a parenthesised E. A plus can appear only at E level and a times only at T level, so × binds tighter than +. The left recursion E → E + T makes + left associative; T → T × F makes × left associative. Some syllabi call this conversion 'ambiguous CFG to unambiguous CFG'.

For id + id × id the only tree has E → E + T at the root. The left E becomes id. The right T becomes T × F, with both T and F becoming id. The leaves are id, +, id, ×, id. With id values 1, 2, 3 the value is 1 + 2 × 3 = 7.

items: Put the lowest-precedence operator in the start variable, for example E for +.
Add a new variable for the next higher precedence, for example T for ×; let E use T.
Continue down to atoms: F → ( E ) | id.
Use left recursion for left associativity and right recursion for right associativity.
If one rule is needed in two places, add a new start symbol and keep the old variable for the inner use.

blocks.text: A context-free language L is inherently ambiguous if every context-free grammar that generates L is ambiguous. This is a property of L, not of a chosen grammar.
L = { aⁱ bʲ cᵏ | i = j or j = k, with i, j, k ≥ 0 }
blocks.where: aⁱ means i copies of a, bʲ means j copies of b, and cᵏ means k copies of c.

blocks.text: A grammar must provide one mechanism that matches a with b and another that matches b with c. Strings with i = j and j = k, that is aⁿbⁿcⁿ, need both mechanisms at once. Any single grammar has to overlap them, so some string gets two trees.
L = { aⁿ bⁿ cᵐ dᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 } ∪ { aⁿ bᵐ cᵐ dⁿ | n, m ≥ 0 }
blocks.where: The two parts share strings such as aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ when n = m, and the same overlap forces ambiguity.

blocks.text: The full proofs use the pumping lemma for context-free languages (see 3.6); they are not asked in this chapter. For a given CFG, deciding whether it is ambiguous is undecidable; Unit 6 covers that result.

figure.caption: The same string, id + id × id, has two parse trees. In the first the plus rule is at the root; in the second the times rule is, so the groupings give 7 and 9.

spec.aria: Two parse trees for the same string: in one the plus is at the root, in the other the multiplication is, so the two groupings compute different values.

examples.question: Consider the grammar G: E → E + E | E × E | ( E ) | id. The string is id + id × id, where the first id is 1, the second id is 2 and the third id is 3. (a) Give the two parse trees by their root rules. (b) Compute the value each tree gives. (c) Is G ambiguous? (d) Give the value from the unambiguous layered grammar.
steps: Label the leaves left to right: id₁ = 1, id₂ = 2, id₃ = 3.
Tree A uses root E → E + E. Left subtree is id₁, value 1. Right subtree is id₂ × id₃, value 2 × 3 = 6. Total value 1 + 6 = 7. Grouping: (1) + (2 × 3).
Tree B uses root E → E × E. Left subtree is id₁ + id₂, value 1 + 2 = 3. Right subtree is id₃, value 3. Total value 3 × 3 = 9. Grouping: (1 + 2) × (3).
Both trees derive the same terminal string id + id × id, so G is ambiguous by definition.
The layered grammar E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id has only one tree for this string: plus at the E root and times inside T. Its value is 1 + 2 × 3 = 7.
examples.answer: Tree A gives 7, tree B gives 9, so G is ambiguous; the layered unambiguous grammar gives 7.
examples.check:
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
print(a + b * c)
print((a + b) * c)

traps: Two different derivations of the same tree are not ambiguity. Only two different parse trees count; compare leftmost derivations.
An ambiguous grammar does not make its language inherently ambiguous. The language may have another unambiguous grammar.
Precedence levels do not fix associativity by themselves. Use left recursion for left associativity and right recursion for right associativity.
Do not drop the factor rule F → ( E ) | id when layering; without it the grammar cannot derive parenthesised strings or identifiers.

quiz.a: A CFG G is ambiguous if some string in L(G) has two different parse trees.

quiz.q: Why is E → E + E | E × E | ( E ) | id ambiguous for id + id × id?
quiz.a: The plus rule and the times rule can both be the root, giving trees for (id) + (id × id) and (id + id) × (id).

quiz.q: In E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id, give the value of id + id × id with id values 1, 2, 3.
quiz.a: The only tree groups the string as 1 + (2 × 3), so the value is 7.

quiz.q: Convert G: E → E + E | E × E | id to an unambiguous grammar with × before + and both left associative.
quiz.a: Use E → E + T | T; T → T × F | F; F → id.

quiz.q: A grammar for L is ambiguous. Can you conclude L is inherently ambiguous?
quiz.a: No. Inherent ambiguity requires every grammar for L to be ambiguous. Fix the given grammar and test again.

quiz.q: Why does {aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k} force ambiguity in any grammar?
quiz.a: Strings with i = j = k satisfy both conditions. A grammar needs two overlapping matching mechanisms, and at aⁿbⁿcⁿ both apply, so some string gets two trees.

quiz.q: Is ambiguity of a given CFG decidable?
quiz.a: No, it is undecidable; see Unit 6.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as yacc and ANTLR report shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflicts that often come from ambiguous rules; GLR parsers accept ambiguous grammars and return several trees. Natural-language parsers expect ambiguity because a sentence can have several readings. In formal language theory, inherent ambiguity connects to deterministic context-free languages and to parsing complexity. Search for 'inherently ambiguous context-free language' and 'ambiguous grammar undecidable'.
